newsitem.title: UK: Euro currency may cost retailers 22 bln stg -- FT.
newsitem.headline: Euro currency may cost retailers 22 bln stg -- FT.

text.p: Switching to a single European currency could burden European Union retailers with costs of more than 27 billion Ecu (22 billion stg), the Financial Times said on Friday.
Quoting estimates from EU retailing body EuroCommerce, the newspaper said British retailers alone could face a 3.5 billion stg bill if the UK opted to join the European Monetary Union (EMU).
In a research report, EuroCommerce claimed that most European retailers were in favour of EMU.

But EuroCommerce added in its report: "It would be politically difficult to sell the euro (single currency) to citizens if high costs were imposed on companies, and if, as a result, prices would increase."

The Financial Times said the EuroCommerce report showed that there were important issues to be resolved with EMU, notably whether the new currency would be introduced in one "big bang" rapid switchover, or staggered over six months.
Under the planned EMU transition scenario, the euro will be introduced in 1999 for banks, financial markets and governments. But national currencies will remain in circulation until 2002.
EuroCommerce studied two options: first, a six-month transition to a single currency in 2002 and second, the alternative "big bang" switchover.
The Financial Times said EuroCommerce estimated that the staggered introduction would cost EU retailers 27 billion ecu -- or almost two percent of their annual turnover.

About five billion ecu of this would stem from the problems of handling two currencies in the shops and a further four billion from the dual display of prices. The rest would arise from computer changes, staff training and public campaigns.
EuroCommerce believes that a "big bang" would cut the bill to 17 billion Ecu.
